claims.claim: Oliver says the formal, scholarly, distant history is presumably the authoritative one yet is placed in the margins of the text.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, 'History in the Margins: Epigraphs and Negative Space in Robin Hobb's Assassin's Apprentice', Mythlore 41.1 (2022), pp. 45-66
claims.quote: the formal, scholarly, distant history is presumably the primary one

claims.claim: Oliver says the first chapter's epigraph opens with the authoritative voice of History establishing a clear centre to its narrative.
claims.quote: opens with the authoritative voice of History

claims.claim: Oliver observes that the chapter thirteen epigraph on Patience includes evidentiary quotes from her nursemaids and publicly available information rather than the author's own experience of her.
claims.quote: he includes evidentiary quotes from her nursemaids and publicly available information

claims.claim: Oliver calls the history that opens the Patience chapter dry, impersonal, but objective, and judges the personal main text more authoritative and satisfying.
claims.quote: the dry, impersonal, but objective history beginning the chapter

claims.claim: Oliver names Hobb's most striking stylistic element negative narration: describing what is not happening instead of or before what is happening.
claims.quote: describing what is not happening instead of or before describing

claims.claim: Oliver says the negative narration shows up in sentences that start by telling what a character is not doing or feeling.
claims.quote: sentences that start by telling what a character is not doing

claims.claim: Oliver says the novel constantly focuses on what is not happening or not present in order to define what is happening.
claims.quote: focuses on what is not happening or what is not present

claims.claim: Oliver argues that only through absences and the things that did not happen can the reader apprehend what did happen.
claims.quote: Only through absences, the negative spaces, the things that did not happen

claims.claim: Oliver identifies a roughly seventy-page stretch of the novel as narrative given over to describing what is not there.
claims.quote: the narrative given over to describing what is not there

claims.claim: Oliver says that when Fitz shifts from a discourse of history to a discourse of fantasy the style shifts to extensive parataxis, elevated figurative language, and parallelism.
claims.quote: extensive parataxis, elevated figurative language, and parallelism

claims.claim: Oliver says the later epigraphs become increasingly infected by the style of imaginative fiction in place of the style of scholarly discourse.
claims.quote: the epigraphs become increasingly infected by the style of imaginative fiction

claims.claim: Oliver counts two sentences using inverted syntax in the chapter fifteen epigraph, alongside parataxis across sentence boundaries and listed parallel phrases.
Mendlesohn, quoted by Oliver, likens each chapter's opening memoir to the Venerable Bede's history and calls it recollection and gossip masquerading as an accurate description of the past.
claims.source: Farah Mendlesohn, Rhetorics of Fantasy (2008), p. 16, quoted by Matthew Oliver in Mythlore 41.1 (2022)
claims.quote: recollection and gossip masquerading as an accurate description of the past

claims.claim: Hobb says she tries to keep in mind that every character is the hero of his own story.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Syl R. Martin, 2023
claims.quote: every character is the hero of his own story

claims.claim: Hobb says each character has to be the product of the imaginary world they exist in.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Syl R. Martin, 2023
claims.quote: the product of the imaginary world they exist in

verdicts.trueWording: presumably the primary one, the authoritative one
verdicts.note: p.46 (PDF via Wayback raw capture): 'the formal, scholarly, distant history is presumably the primary one, the authoritative one, yet it is placed in the margins of the text'. Both limbs (authoritative; placed in the margins) supported verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: opens with the authoritative voice of History
verdicts.note: p.53: 'the epigraph to the first chapter opens with the authoritative voice of History establishing a clear center to its narrative'. Claim's 'centre' is a spelling variant of the page's 'center'.

verdicts.trueWording: Instead, he includes evidentiary quotes from her nursemaids
verdicts.note: p.56: 'Chapter 13 ... opens with an epigraph describing his father's widow, Patience. This lengthy excerpt contains no hint of the author's relationship to her or that any information in it came from his experience of her. Instead, he includes evidentiary quotes from her nursemaids and publicly available information.' All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: the main text feels more authoritative and satisfying
verdicts.note: pp.56-57: 'The "marginalia" here (that is, the main text) feels more authoritative and satisfying than the dry, impersonal, but objective history beginning the chapter'. Both limbs supported; Oliver's verb is 'feels', which the claim renders as 'judges'. Quote actually sits at the p.56/57 break, not p.56 alone (citation field only).

verdicts.trueWording: Perhaps the most striking stylistic element ... 'negative narration'
verdicts.note: p.57: 'Perhaps the most striking stylistic element of this book is its continual insistence on describing what is not happening instead of or before describing what is happening, a style we might think of as "negative narration."' Both limbs supported; note Oliver hedges ('Perhaps', 'we might think of as') where the claim asserts flatly.

verdicts.trueWording: in sentences that start by telling what a character is not doing
verdicts.note: p.57: 'This manifests not just in double negatives (of which there are many) but in sentences that start by telling what a character is not doing or feeling.' Verbatim, including the 'or feeling' limb.

verdicts.trueWording: constantly focuses on what is not happening or what is not present
verdicts.note: p.45: 'the novel constantly focuses on what is not happening or what is not present in order to define what is happening by evoking it in imagination.' Every limb verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: can we imagine and apprehend what did happen
verdicts.note: p.47: 'Only through absences, the negative spaces, the things that did not happen, can we imagine and apprehend what did happen'. Claim's 'the reader' stands for Oliver's inclusive 'we'; page adds 'imagine and' before 'apprehend'.

verdicts.trueWording: a lengthy portion of the narrative given over to describing what is not there
verdicts.note: p.61: 'In a way, this is a lengthy portion of the narrative given over to describing what is not there' (the 'misted' section where Galen's tampering is the absent detail). The seventy-page limb is supported two paragraphs later, pp.61-62: 'Then Verity finally explicates what has been happening for the past 70 pages of the novel' — same stretch, but the figure and the phrase are not in one sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: particularly extensive parataxis, elevated figurative language, and parallelism
verdicts.note: pp.59-60: 'His description employs several syntactic patterns typical of the elevated style associated with fantasy novels, particularly extensive parataxis, elevated figurative language, and parallelism', and 'Fitz marks his shift from a discourse of history to a discourse of fantasy with a shift in style.' Both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: increasingly infected by the style of imaginative fiction
verdicts.note: pp.60-61: 'the epigraphs become increasingly infected by the style of imaginative fiction in place of the style of scholarly discourse', in a passage about the novel's later movement ('Even as the narrator starts to shift the burden of constructing events to the reader'). A first literal string match missed only because pypdf breaks the word as 'imag inative' at a line end.

verdicts.trueWording: Two sentences use inverted syntax (the first and the last)
verdicts.note: pp.62-63, on the chapter 15 epigraph about the Skill: 'Two sentences use inverted syntax (the first and the last), in addition to the parataxis across sentence boundaries ("And this is the thing") and the listing of parallel phrases'. All three limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: a memoir not dissimilar to the Venerable Bede's history
verdicts.note: p.63, Oliver's block quotation of Mendlesohn: 'Each chapter begins with a memoir not dissimilar to the Venerable Bede's history: recollection and gossip masquerading as an accurate description of the past.' Cited '(16)' and Works Cited gives 'Mendlesohn, Farah. Rhetorics of Fantasy. Wesleyan UP, 2008.' — attribution, year and page all check out.

verdicts.trueWording: I try to keep in mind that every character is the hero of his own story
verdicts.note: Raw HTML of sylrmartin.com (200, live, no summarizer): 'I try to keep in mind that every character is the hero of his own story, that is, he brings his own past, his problems, his attitude and his hope for the future to the story.' Attributed to ROBIN HOBB answering SRM; page datePublished 2023-05-19.

verdicts.trueWording: Each character has to be the product of the imaginary world they exist in
verdicts.note: Same live page, inspiration answer: 'But I never take a person I know, change name and hair colour and insert into a book. It just wouldn't work. Each character has to be the product of the imaginary world they exist in.' Verbatim, Hobb speaking.
